name: Ferrochem AcidWall Pro MK-4 Full Enclosure Suit
description:
Full-body enclosure suit in corroded-mustard yellow with black chemical-resistance banding at all seams. Triple-laminate shell of vulcanized polyimide over woven aramid, with a bonded inner moisture-wicking membrane. Visor hood integrates a filtered air intake mounted left-shoulder. Common on Shelf salvage crews working flooded industrial basements where acid pooling is standard.

Seam tape is factory-applied in neon orange — when it fades to white, the suit's primary seal integrity is compromised. Most Shelf workers ignore this. Wrist and ankle cuffs cinch via ratchet buckles, leaving room for basic chrome cuffs beneath.
functionality: Rated for pH 1–13 splash and immersion up to 40 minutes. Integrated shoulder air-intake runs through a replaceable carbon-block filter cartridge. Ratchet cuff seals accommodate basic chrome prosthetics. Internal BCI port slot on hood collar allows neural comms while fully enclosed.
what_it_says: You work in places that will kill you slowly, and you know exactly how much protection you can actually afford.
story_hooks: A salvager's suit seal tape has been white for three weeks — she can't afford a replacement and is showing early acid-burn scarring on her wrists.
A batch of counterfeit MK-4 suits hit the Shelf market — identical labeling, half the chemical resistance rating, and workers are dying.
Someone found a sealed MK-4 suit in a flooded basement with a body inside — the suit is undamaged, but the person inside died of something else entirely.

physical_description.visual_profile: A bulky, utilitarian full-body enclosure that reads as industrial hazmat gear—protective and imposing. The corroded-mustard yellow gives it a worn, industrial aesthetic even when new. The integrated visor hood and shoulder-mounted air intake create an almost insectoid silhouette. On the wearer, it commands space and signals danger-adjacent work.
physical_description.fit: Relaxed and intentionally loose to accommodate layering and basic augmentations (chrome cuffs, subcutaneous gear). Articulated at shoulders, elbows, and hips for mobility despite the bulk. Tapered at wrists and ankles with ratchet buckles that cinch tight for seal integrity.
physical_description.primary_material: Triple-laminate shell: vulcanized polyimide outer layer bonded to woven aramid middle, with bonded inner moisture-wicking membrane. Factory seam tape in neon orange (fading to white as integrity degrades).
physical_description.texture: Smooth synthetic shell with subtle texture from the aramid weave visible under magnification. Seam tape has slight raised profile. Ratchet buckles are cold metal. Inner membrane feels slightly tacky and moisture-resistant.
physical_description.color_scheme: Corroded-mustard yellow as primary, with black chemical-resistance banding at all seams. Neon orange seam tape (degrading to white over time). Matte finish from industrial use.
physical_description.closures: Ratchet buckles at wrists and ankles. Full-body zipper down the front (industrial-grade, likely corroded). No other traditional fasteners—designed for quick donning/doffing.
distinctive_features: Integrated visor hood with filtered air intake mounted on left shoulder
Factory neon-orange seam tape (fades white when seal integrity compromises)
Triple-laminate construction visible at torn edges
Ratchet buckles allow chrome cuff accommodation beneath
Corroded finish suggesting heavy industrial use
Black chemical-resistance banding reinforce all high-stress seams
physical_description.tier_indicator: Tier 5 salvage/Tier 4 working-class. Gray-market surplus industrial equipment. Affordable to street crews but not aspirational.
physical_description.cultural_context: Shelf worker, salvage crew, acid-flooded industrial basement explorer. Wearing this signals you work in hazardous conditions for subsistence wages. It's practical, not fashionable—a uniform of necessity rather than choice.
physical_description.condition_typical: Weathered and corroded. Seam tape faded to white (ignored). Possible tears or patched sections. Visor scratched from debris. Ratchet buckles stiff from salt corrosion. Stains from acid splash or mineral deposits. Despite wear, still functional because it was built cheap and durable.
